The abdominal wall is a stack of layers with predictable fibre directions, and almost every surgical decision about it — incision direction, closure tension, trocar placement — follows from knowing which layer you are in and which way its fibres run.

7–12Ribs forming the upper border
T10Dermatome at the umbilicus
L3–L4Vertebral level of umbilicus
1/3Umbilicus–pubis distance to arcuate line
Boundaries

Where the wall begins and ends

Above, the lower rib margin; below, the iliac crests, inguinal ligaments and pubic bones; posterolaterally it ends at the lumbar spine and its muscles.

Fibre direction

Transverse dominance

Dermal fibres run mostly transversely along a gently upward-curving line, so a vertical incision is held under more tension and heals to a wider scar.

Two muscle groups

Midline and flank

Vertical midline muscles (rectus abdominis, pyramidalis) and three flat flank muscles whose aponeuroses fuse across the midline to build the rectus sheath.

Entry point

The umbilicus

All layers fuse here, which makes it the usual endoscopic entry — and puts it directly over the aortic bifurcation and the iliac vein confluence.

Principle

Because the flank muscles pull transversely, a vertical suture line in the rectus sheath sits under more tension than a transverse one — which is why vertical incisions are more prone to dehiscence.

The layers, outside in

Abdominal wall layers, compiled from the chapter narrative
LayerCharacterSurgical note
SkinDermal fibres predominantly transverseVertical incisions scar wider

Subcutaneous — membranous layer (formerly Scarpa)Fibrous tissue predominates near the sheathBest developed laterally; seen at the lateral ends of low transverse incisions
MusculoaponeuroticRectus and pyramidalis plus three flank muscles and their aponeurosesThe load-bearing closure layer
Transversalis fasciaFibrous lining of the abdominopelvic cavityLast layer crossed for extraperitoneal entry to the retropubic space

PeritoneumSingle epithelial layer with supporting connective tissue (serosa)Carries five infraumbilical folds toward the umbilicus
Why the fatty and membranous layers are regions, not sheets

Neither is a discrete, well-defined layer. They describe regions within one continuous subcutaneous tissue in which the ratio of fat to fibrous septa shifts — fat-dominant superficially, fibrous-dominant close to the rectus sheath. The membranous layer is not seen as a defined layer in a midline vertical incision at all; it is most evident at the lateral borders of a low transverse incision, just above the sheath.

The chapter's own tabulated summary of these layers is Table 1.1, so the table above was reconstructed from the surrounding narrative instead. That is a production error in the book file, not a pairing error here, so the mislabelled image has been left out rather than presented as Table 1.1.

Working from skin to peritoneum, each layer has a characteristic feel, a characteristic attachment, and a characteristic way of going wrong.

Step walkthrough

Crossing the lower abdominal wall, layer by layer

Step 1 of 5 · Flank muscles

External oblique first

The most superficial flat muscle. Fibres run obliquely downward and forward from the lower eight ribs to the iliac crest, pubic tubercle and linea alba.

  • Its thickened lower free edge forms the inguinal ligament.
  • It becomes aponeurotic around the midclavicular line — and more laterally as you move down.
Step 2 of 5 · Deeper flank layers

Internal oblique and transversus abdominis

Internal oblique fibres fan upward and medially and are generally perpendicular to the external oblique — but in the lower abdomen they arch caudally and run in a similar direction to it.

  • The caudal transversus fuses with internal oblique as the conjoint tendon (inguinal falx).
  • That fusion is why only two layers are discernible at the lateral end of a low transverse incision.
Step 3 of 5 · Rectus sheath

The arcuate line changes everything

Above the arcuate line the sheath splits to lie both in front of and behind the rectus. In the lower quarter it lies entirely anterior, and the rectus muscle sits directly on transversalis fascia.

  • Transition point: about one-third of the way from umbilicus to pubic crest.
  • A vertical incision reaching the umbilicus therefore has to divide the posterior sheath.
Step 4 of 5 · Peritoneum

Five folds converge on the umbilicus

  • One median umbilical fold over the median umbilical ligament (urachal remnant).
  • Paired medial umbilical folds over the obliterated umbilical arteries.
  • Paired lateral umbilical folds over the inferior epigastric vessels — transecting these bleeds significantly.

The bladder reflection is triangular with its apex highest in the midline, so opening the peritoneum lateral to the midline is less likely to injure the bladder.

Step 5 of 5 · Lateral landmark

Round ligament and the deep ring

Trace the round ligament to where it enters the deep inguinal ring: the inferior epigastric vessels lie just medial to that point.

  • The round ligament passes lateral to the deep inferior epigastric vessels, through the canal, to the labium majus.
  • The ilioinguinal nerve and the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve also run in the canal.
Rectus abdominis

Three to four tendinous inscriptions

Sternum and costal cartilages 5–7 to the anterior pubic bone. At each inscription the sheath is firmly attached to muscle, so the two are hard to separate.

Pyramidalis

Highly variable, firmly midline

From the pubic bones anterior to rectus into the linea alba a few centimetres above the symphysis. Its midline grip makes blunt separation here difficult.

Transversalis fascia

The extraperitoneal gateway

Visible suprapubically just under the rectus muscles; incised or bluntly swept off the bladder to take tissues down by layers into the retropubic space.

Umbilical ring

A defect in the linea alba

The window the fetal umbilical vessels used, and the route umbilical hernias take. The umbilical fascia behind it is a thickening of transversalis fascia.

Pearl

The membranous layer is best developed laterally. Expect to see it at the lateral borders of a low transverse incision just above the rectus sheath, and not at all in a midline vertical incision.

The umbilicus as a landmark — what sits behind it

The umbilicus usually lies at the junction of the third and fourth lumbar vertebrae. That is also the level at which the iliac veins join to form the vena cava and at which the aorta bifurcates. Its skin is supplied by T10. The round ligament of the liver and the median and medial umbilical ligaments attach to the ring in inconsistent arrangements.

The rectus sheath is not one structure but two arrangements, divided by the arcuate line.

Above the arcuate line

The sheath splits around the rectus. Anterior layer from external oblique plus the split aponeurosis of internal oblique; posterior layer from transversus abdominis plus the other half of the internal oblique aponeurosis.

At the arcuate line

Roughly one-third of the way from umbilicus to pubic crest, which lies medial to the pubic tubercle.

Below the arcuate line

All aponeuroses pass in front. There is no posterior sheath; the rectus muscle lies in direct contact with transversalis fascia.

In the midline

Above the line the linea alba unites anterior and posterior layers, so sharp dissection is usually needed to separate them during a Pfannenstiel incision.

Pearl

The linea semilunaris is not simply where the three flank layers fuse — what happens at that line differs above and below the arcuate line, and a hernia through it is a Spigelian (lateral-ventral) hernia.

The flank muscles in detail

External oblique

Down and forward

Ribs 5–12 to iliac crest, pubic tubercle and linea alba. Free posterior edge of its aponeurosis is the inguinal ligament.

Internal oblique

Up and medial

Anterior two-thirds of iliac crest, lateral inguinal ligament and thoracolumbar fascia to ribs 10–12, pecten pubis and linea alba.

Transversus abdominis

Transverse throughout

Costal cartilages 7–12, thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest and lateral third of the inguinal ligament to pubic crest, pecten pubis and linea alba.

Conjoint tendon

Behind the superficial ring

Fused caudal transversus and internal oblique. With transversalis fascia it forms the posterior wall of the inguinal canal; weakening gives a direct inguinal hernia.

Watch for

The linea semilunaris runs from the ninth costal cartilage to the pubic tubercle and marks the lateral border of the rectus. Incisions along that border risk denervating the muscle.

The inguinal canal — boundaries and contents

The canal lies at the lower edge of the musculofascial layer, superior and parallel to the inguinal ligament. The midinguinal point is halfway between the symphysis and the anterosuperior iliac spine, and the femoral pulse is palpable there. It has superficial and deep rings.

  • Roof: inferior free edge of transversus abdominis and internal oblique fibres.
  • Posterior wall: conjoint tendon with transversalis fascia.
  • Contents in the woman: round ligament to the labium majus, ilioinguinal nerve, genital branch of genitofemoral nerve.
  • Failure of the processus vaginalis to regress allows an indirect hernia through the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.

Superficial and deep vessels run parallel courses toward the umbilicus, which is exactly why a single line drawn from the femoral pulse to the umbilicus predicts both.

Vessels

Skin and subcutaneous tissue

  • Superficial epigastric — diagonal, from the femoral vessels toward the umbilicus, branching widely as it nears it. Sits midway between skin and musculofascial layer, on the line from femoral pulse to umbilicus.
  • External pudendal — runs medially to the mons pubis, with many midline branches; bleeding in its territory is heavier than elsewhere in the abdominal subcutaneous tissue.
  • Superficial circumflex iliac — laterally from the femoral vessels toward the flank.

Musculofascial layer

  • Inferior epigastric (from external iliac) with two veins — originates lateral to the rectus, runs diagonally toward the umbilicus, crossing the muscle's lateral border midway between pubis and umbilicus, then lies on the muscle's dorsal surface between it and the posterior sheath, branching so there is no longer a single trunk.
  • Deep circumflex iliac — lies between internal oblique and transversus abdominis.
  • Around the umbilicus the inferior epigastric anastomoses with the superior epigastric, a branch of the internal thoracic artery.
Principle

The epigastric vessels lie about 5.5 cm from the midline just above the symphysis and about 4.5 cm from the midline at the umbilicus. Placing a trocar either lateral or medial to the line joining those two points minimises vascular injury.

Nerves

  • Supply comes from the abdominal continuation of intercostal nerves 7–11, the subcostal nerve (T12), and the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves (both L1).
  • Each intercostal nerve gives a lateral cutaneous branch, pierces the lateral border of the rectus sheath, sends a branch into the rectus, then perforates the sheath as anterior cutaneous branches to skin.
  • Between internal oblique and transversus lies a neurovascular plane equivalent to the intercostal plane, carrying the nerves and arteries of the anterolateral wall.
Hesselbach triangle and direct hernias

The angle between the inferior epigastric vessels and the lateral border of the rectus forms the apex of the inguinal (Hesselbach) triangle, whose base is the inguinal ligament. Direct inguinal hernias protrude through this area, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels — the distinction from the indirect hernia, which passes through the deep ring lateral to those vessels.

Seeing the vessels intraoperatively

The inferior epigastric vessels can often be seen directly through the peritoneum at laparoscopy. In thin patients the superficial epigastric vessels can frequently be identified by transillumination. Where neither is visible, the round ligament traced to the deep inguinal ring gives the landmark: the vessels lie just medial to it.

Six nerves account for most of the neurologic morbidity of gynecologic surgery, and each has a single characteristic position where it is vulnerable.

Classification explorer

Nerves at risk in pelvic surgery

Select a nerve for its root value, course, the manoeuvre that injures it, and the resulting deficit.

Positioning hazard

Three branches — femoral, lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh, and the femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve — pass under the inguinal ligament and can be compressed in lithotomy. In vaginal surgery, femoral nerve injury is most often attributed to positioning rather than dissection.

Retractor-related injuries in one place
  • Genitofemoral — direct pressure where it lies on psoas.
  • Lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh — a blade placed lateral to psoas.
  • Femoral — compression by the lateral blades of a self-retaining retractor.

All three share the same remedy: check blade position against the psoas muscle rather than against the wound edge.

Most abdominal wall complications are anatomical rather than technical — they follow from an incision or a suture crossing a line it should have stopped short of.

Principle

Low transverse fascial incisions should not extend beyond the lateral margins of the rectus muscles, and suture purchases should not extend lateral to the incision edges — both cross the neurovascular plane and risk nerve entrapment and inferior epigastric injury.

Entrapment

Iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal

Caught by a lateral suture purchase or cut at closure or accessory trocar insertion. Pain may declare itself months to years later.

Denervation

Incisions at the rectus border

An incision along the lateral border of the rectus denervates the muscle, which can render it atrophic and weaken the whole wall.

Cutaneous anaesthesia

The Pfannenstiel perforating nerve

Elevating the sheath off the muscle stretches the perforating nerve; it is sometimes ligated or cauterised for haemostasis, leaving an anaesthetic patch of skin.

Bleeding

Lateral umbilical folds

These cover the inferior epigastric vessels. Transecting them can cause significant bleeding.

How to avoid it
  • Place lateral trocars superior to the anterosuperior iliac spines.
  • Keep low transverse fascial incisions within the lateral borders of the rectus muscles.
  • Identify and spare nerves within the neurovascular plane where it is possible to do so.
  • Open the peritoneum lateral to the midline, where the bladder reflection sits lower.
Why a vertical incision behaves differently

Two separate facts compound. At skin level, transversely oriented dermal fibres put a vertical incision under more tension and produce a wider scar. At fascial level, the transverse orientation and transverse pull of the flank muscles place vertical suture lines in the rectus sheath under more tension than transverse ones, making vertical incisions more prone to dehiscence. A vertical incision reaching or passing the umbilicus also obliges you to incise the posterior sheath.

The anterior perineal triangle is layered much like the abdominal wall — skin, subcutaneous tissue, then a fascial sheet — and its fibrous attachments decide where blood and infection can travel.

S2–S4Pudendal nerve origin
3–4 cmLength of each vestibular bulb
11 & 1O’clock position, dorsal nerve of clitoris
12–20Superficial inguinal nodes
Two triangles

A shared base between the tuberosities

Anterior and posterior perineal triangles meet along a line between the ischial tuberosities. Outer borders are the bony outlet: pubic arch and ischiopubic rami in front, sacrotuberous ligament and coccyx behind.

Roof

One superior boundary for both

The inferior fascia of the levator ani muscles forms the superior boundary of both the anterior and the posterior triangle.

Layered plan

Familiar from the abdomen

Skin and subcutaneous tissue overlying a fascial layer — here the perineal membrane, which separates the superficial from the deep perineal pouch.

Naming

Old terms retired

Perineal membrane replaces urogenital diaphragm; membranous layer replaces Colles fascia; bulbospongiosus replaces bulbocavernosus.

Principle

The subcutaneous septa attach laterally to the ischiopubic rami and fuse posteriorly with the perineal membrane, but there is no anterior attachment to the pubic rami — so a hematoma or infection deep to the membranous layer is contained posterolaterally but free to track into the abdominal wall.

Subcutaneous regions of the vulva, and what each implies
RegionCompositionClinical consequence
Fatty layer (superficial)Fat predominates; continuous with the abdominal wall fat, carrying smooth muscle and the round ligament terminationNo containing attachments; spread between perineum and abdomen is possible
Membranous layer (deep, formerly Colles)Less fat, prominent interlacing fibrous septaAttachments to ischiopubic rami and perineal membrane limit posterolateral spread
Labia minora / vestibuleNo adipose base; loose connective tissue stratumSkin mobile and easily dissected off during skinning vulvectomy
Subcutaneous emphysema at laparoscopy

Because the abdominal and perineal subcutaneous layers communicate anteriorly, carbon dioxide that extravasates into the subcutaneous layer — with accidental trocar displacement or during lengthy procedures — can produce emphysema extending from the abdominal wall down into the perineum. The same continuity explains spread of hematoma or infection in either direction.

The vulva lies on the pubic bones and extends posteriorly under the pubic arch, and each of its named parts carries its own set of lesions.

Classification explorer

Structures of the vulva

Select a structure for its composition, relations and the pathology that arises there.

Pearl

Because the labia minora and vestibule sit on loose connective tissue rather than on fat, their skin lifts readily off the underlying tissue — the property that makes skinning vulvectomy feasible in that region.

Variation, symptoms and labial reduction

Shape and size of the labia minora vary greatly. One or both may extend well beyond the labia majora and be drawn into the vagina during coitus or other activity. Where that is associated with dyspareunia or pain, surgical reduction may be considered. Complications include hypoesthesia and paresthesias. Procedures that remove the prepuce or adjacent skin and underlying connective tissue risk injuring the dorsal nerve of the clitoris.

The perineal membrane is the reference plane: everything caudal to it is the superficial pouch, everything just deep to it is the deep pouch.

Superficial pouch

Between investing fascia and membrane

Contains the clitoris and its crura, the vestibular bulbs, and the ischiocavernosus and bulbospongiosus muscles. The erectile bodies lie on the caudal surface of the perineal membrane.

Deep pouch

Just deep to the membrane

Holds the compressor urethrae and sphincter urethrovaginalis — the striated urogenital sphincter muscles that arch over the urethra.

Perineal fascia

One covering, three muscles

Bulbospongiosus, ischiocavernosus and superficial transverse perineal are all covered by perineal fascia, which is continuous with the clitoral fascia.

Posterior triangle

Ischioanal fossa

Bounded superomedially by levator ani and laterally by obturator internus, with the pudendal canal and neurovascular bundle on its lateral wall.

Muscles of the superficial pouch

  • Ischiocavernosus — from the ischial tuberosities and the free surfaces of the crura, inserting on the upper crura and often on the clitoral body.
  • Bulbospongiosus — originates in the perineal body and partially covers the vestibular bulbs.
  • Superficial transverse perineal — a few fibres arising with ischiocavernosus from the ischial tuberosity, running transversely toward the lateral margins of the perineal body.

Ischiocavernosus and bulbospongiosus both insert into the body of the clitoris and act to pull it downward.

Pearl

The perineal membrane is not a two-layered structure with muscle between, which is why the term urogenital diaphragm was abandoned. It lies just caudal to the skeletal muscle of the striated urogenital sphincter.

The clitoris is a midline body topped by the glans with paired crura, and unlike the penis it has no functional relationship to the urethra.

Origin

Embryologically derived from the genital tubercle; homologous with the penis.

Crura

Bend downward from the body, firmly attached to the pubic bones, continuing dorsally on the inferior aspects of the ischiopubic rami before joining in the midline.

Body

Paired corpora cavernosa separated in the midline by the septum of the corpora cavernosa; corpora and crura are invested by the tunica albuginea.

Suspension

The body is suspended from the pubic bones by the subcutaneous suspensory and fundiform ligaments. The fundiform ligament descends from the linea alba above the symphysis, splits around the body, then fuses with the clitoral fascia.

Vestibular bulbs

Paired 3–4 cm masses of richly vascular spongy erectile tissue immediately under the vestibular skin, joining anteriorly at the commissure of the bulbs where the tissue attaches to the undersurface of the glans and body.

Autonomic innervation

  • Erectile tissue is supplied by the cavernous nerves of the clitoris, distal extensions of the uterovaginal plexus — itself a component of the inferior hypogastric plexus.
  • These fibres run in paravaginal and paraurethral connective tissue and reach the perineum by passing under the pubic bones, joining the dorsal nerve of the clitoris to supply the corpora cavernosa.
  • They are of very small calibre and can only be confirmed microscopically. They carry both sympathetic and parasympathetic components and are critical to sexual function.
Watch for

Injury to the inferior hypogastric plexus during radical hysterectomy or other extensive pelvic or perineal surgery can cause varying degrees of voiding, sexual and defecatory dysfunction. Anti-incontinence procedures that pass sutures or trocars through paraurethral tissue may disrupt the same fibres within the retropubic space.

Where the dorsal nerve sits relative to the fascial layers

The dorsal nerve and vessels of the clitoris lie outside the tunica albuginea but within the clitoral fascia, which is continuous with the deep part of the suspensory ligament. Along the dorsal surface of the body the nerve remains deep to the clitoral fascia and superficial to the tunica albuginea, giving small branches to the prepuce skin and to the corpora cavernosa before perforating the glans.

The pudendal nerve is the main sensory and motor nerve of the perineum, and its vessels run the same course throughout.

Step walkthrough

Course of the pudendal nerve and vessels

Step 1 of 3 · Territory

What it has to reach

The nerve arises from the sacral plexus (S2–S4); the accompanying arteries arise from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery.

  • Sensation to the external genitalia.
  • Motor supply to the superficial perineal muscles, parts of the striated urethral sphincter, and the external anal sphincter.
Step 2 of 3 · Exit and re-entry

Around the ischial spine, into Alcock canal

  • Leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, passing behind the sacrospinous ligament just medial to the ischial spine.
  • Enters the pudendal (Alcock) canal through the lesser sciatic foramen.
  • The canal is formed by a splitting of the obturator fascia over the medial surface of obturator internus, running roughly from the ischial spine to the ischial tuberosity.
Step 3 of 3 · Terminal branches

Three branches, three territories

The dorsal nerve of the clitoris stays in the deep pouch adherent to the inner surface of the ischiopubic ramus, perforates the perineal membrane, then runs on the deep surface of ischiocavernosus and the crus.

  • About 2–3 cm lateral to the mid symphysis it emerges from the deep lateral surface of the crus.
  • Consistently 2–4 mm in diameter in that region.
  • Runs on the dorsal clitoral body at roughly the 11 and 1 o’clock positions.
Terminal branches of the pudendal nerve
BranchSuppliesInjury matters because
Dorsal nerve of the clitorisPrimarily sensory to the clitoris; branches to prepuce skin and corpora cavernosa; ends by perforating the glansExcisional procedures deep to the subcutaneous tissue in this region, pelvic fractures and some anti-incontinence procedures can affect clitoral sensation and sexual function
Perineal nerve (largest branch)Posterior labial nerves to the labia minora and most of the labia majora; motor to ischiocavernosus, bulbospongiosus and superficial transverse perineal; sensory to vestibular bulbs, vestibule and lower vaginaCarries most of the motor supply of the superficial pouch
Inferior anal (rectal) nerveExternal anal sphincter and perianal skin; cutaneous supply of the anal canal to the pectinate lineInjury may lead to faecal incontinence and pain syndromes
Anatomical variant

The inferior rectal nerve does not enter the pudendal canal in about 50% of cadaveric specimens examined. That matters in procedures entering the ischioanal fossa and in radiographically guided injections used for pain management.

Contributions to the striated urogenital sphincter

Data are limited, but branches of the perineal nerve may supply the distal part of the striated urogenital sphincter muscles — the compressor urethrae and urethrovaginalis — which lie in the deep perineal pouch superior to the perineal membrane. The dorsal nerve of the clitoris may also contribute branches to these structures.

Vulvar lymphatic drainage runs anteriorly and laterally to the superficial inguinal nodes, and the pattern sets the lateral border of resection for vulvar malignancy.

Superficial inguinal nodes

  • 12–20 nodes in a T-shaped distribution, parallel to and about 1 cm below the inguinal ligament, with the stem running down along the saphenous vein.
  • Often divided into four quadrants centred on the saphenous opening (fossa ovalis).
  • Vulvar drainage goes primarily to the medial nodes of the upper quadrant.
  • They lie deep in the adipose layer of the subcutaneous tissues, in the membranous layer, just superficial to the fascia lata.

Deep inguinal nodes

  • One to three nodes in the femoral canal of the femoral triangle.
  • Reached by lymphatics passing through the saphenous opening in the fascia lata, about 3 cm below the inguinal ligament, lateral to the pubic tubercle.
  • The membranous layer spans that opening as a trabeculated sheet, the cribriform fascia, pierced by lymphatics.
Principle

The lymphatic channels draining tissues outside the hymenal ring lie medial to the labiocrural fold, which establishes that fold as the lateral border of surgical resection for vulvar malignancies.

Pearl

Injection studies show urethral lymphatic drainage terminates in either the right or the left inguinal nodes. The clitoris has been said to drain directly to deep pelvic nodes, bypassing the superficial group, but the clinical significance of this appears minimal.

Superficial vessels crossing the field at groin dissection

Within 2 cm of the inguinal ligament several superficial vessels branch from the saphenous vein and femoral artery as the great saphenous vein joins the femoral vein through the saphenous opening:

  • Superficial epigastric — to the subcutaneous tissues of the lower abdomen.
  • Superficial circumflex iliac — laterally toward the iliac crest.
  • Superficial external pudendal — to the mons, labia majora and prepuce of the clitoris.
Medial thigh compartment — muscles, supply and deficits

One of three anatomic divisions of the thigh; its muscles principally adduct the thigh at the hip.

  • Pectineus — pectineal line of the pubis to the femur; contributes to the floor of the femoral triangle; primary action hip flexion. Transitional between anterior and medial compartments, with dual innervation but primary supply from the femoral nerve.
  • Adductor longus — superior pubic ramus to femur; forms the medial border of the femoral triangle; adducts and flexes.
  • Gracilis — body of pubis and upper half of the inferior ramus to the proximal medial tibia; the most superficial muscle of the compartment; crosses hip and knee.
  • Adductor brevis — beneath adductor longus, between the anterior and posterior branches of the obturator nerve.
  • Adductor magnus — largest and most posterior; adductor part from the ischiopubic ramus, hamstring head from the ischial tuberosity to the medial femoral epicondyle, the latter supplied by the tibial branch of the sciatic nerve.
  • Obturator externus — deep to the adductors; laterally rotates the hip, as obturator internus does.

Blood supply comes from the femoral and obturator arteries; the profunda femoris supplies pectineus and the three adductors, and its medial circumflex femoral branch perforates adductor brevis, obturator externus and gracilis. The obturator artery divides into anterior and posterior branches encircling the obturator membrane. The obturator nerve divides similarly on the anterior and posterior aspects of adductor brevis.

Upright posture put the pelvic outlet at the bottom of the abdominopelvic cavity, and the pelvic floor is the fibromuscular shelf that evolved to close it while still admitting the birth canal.

S3–S5Nerve to the levator ani
2Components of the pelvic diaphragm
3Parts of the external anal sphincter
2–3 cmPerineal body height above the hymenal ring
The design problem

Close the outlet, pass the fetus

The floor must resist downward force yet allow passage of a large, cranially dominant human fetus — so it is a shelf with a cleft, not a sheet.

Two systems

Muscle plus fibrous tethers

A muscular diaphragm with covering fasciae, and a series of visceral ligaments and fasciae holding the organs over the closed parts of that diaphragm.

Weak points

Where the openings are

Ancillary fibrous elements are concentrated over the openings in the pelvic diaphragm and perineal membrane, supporting the viscera exactly where the muscle cannot.

Examination

Standing, not lithotomy

Lithotomy relaxes the musculature. The closure mechanism is best appreciated in the standing patient — and in the nullipara, where a speculum is hard to insert against contracted muscle.

Principle

Textbook depictions of the levator ani are distorted by the extreme abdominal pressures of embalming, which force the muscles downward. Many illustrations therefore fail to show how horizontal this supportive shelf actually is.

Ischioanal fossa — boundaries and contents

In the posterior triangle, the ischioanal fossa lies between the obturator muscle with its medial fascia at the perineal walls, and the levator ani with its inferior fascia.

  • Superomedial boundary: levator ani muscles.
  • Lateral boundary: obturator internus muscle.
  • An anterior recess lies above the perineal membrane.
  • The main part is lateral to levator ani and the external anal sphincter; a posterior part extends above gluteus maximus.
  • The pudendal neurovascular trunk traverses it, with the pudendal canal on its lateral wall.

The perineal membrane is a triangular sheet of dense fibromuscular tissue spanning the anterior half of the pelvic outlet, and it is the reason the posterior vaginal wall and perineal body cannot simply descend.

Step walkthrough

The floor from below upward

Step 1 of 3 · Perineal view

What you see from below

The pelvic diaphragm spans the bony pelvis in two parts: a thin horizontal shelf formed by iliococcygeus, and a thicker U-shaped sling of pubococcygeus and puborectalis around the hiatus.

  • The open area within the U is the levator hiatus, transmitting urethra, vagina and rectum.
  • The part of the hiatus anterior to the perineal body is the urogenital hiatus.
Step 2 of 3 · Deep pouch

Two arch-shaped striated muscles

Just cephalad to the perineal membrane lie two striated muscles that begin posteriorly and pass forward to arch over the urethra.

  • Compressor urethrae and sphincter urethrovaginalis.
  • Both are part of the striated urogenital sphincter and are continuous with the external urethral sphincter; they compress the distal urethra.
  • Posteriorly, skeletal fibres of the transverse vaginal muscle and some smooth muscle intermingle within the membrane itself.
Step 3 of 3 · Attachments

Lateral to bone, medial to viscera

  • Arises from the inner aspect of the inferior ischiopubic rami, superior to the ischiocavernosus muscles and the clitoral crura.
  • Medial attachments: urethra, vaginal walls (roughly at the level of the hymenal ring), and the perineal body.
  • Because of the vagina, it cannot form a continuous sheet closing the anterior pelvis as it does in the man.

By anchoring vagina and perineal body to the bony outlet, it supports the perineal part of the floor against gravity and rises in intra-abdominal pressure.

Pearl

The anterior parts of pubococcygeus and puborectalis lie against the cranial surface of the perineal membrane. Their contraction elevates its medial margin along with the vagina; relaxation allows it to move caudally.

Bedside test

Under anaesthesia, place a finger in the rectum, hook it forward and pull the perineal body gently downward. If the perineal membrane was torn during parturition, an abnormal amount of descent is detectable — the floor sags and the introitus gapes.

The perineal body is the fibromuscular mass bounded by the lower vagina, the perineal skin and the anus — the central point into which many muscles insert.

What attaches to it

Laterally, to bone

Attached to the inferior pubic rami and the ischial tuberosities through the perineal membrane and the superficial transverse perineal muscles.

Anterolaterally

Receives the insertion of the bulbospongiosus muscles.

On its lateral margins

The upper part connects with fibres of the pelvic diaphragm — the puboperinealis portion of pubococcygeus.

Posteriorly

Indirectly attached to the coccyx through the external anal sphincter.

Together these connections anchor the perineal body and its surrounding structures to the bony pelvis and hold it in position.

Naming

The older term central point (tendon) of the perineum is descriptive rather than misleading here — it captures exactly the role of a hub into which multiple muscles insert.

Histology matters

The perineal body encompasses a central fibrous connection between the two halves of the perineal membrane and extends cranially for 2–3 cm above the hymenal ring. Within this segment there is no histological plane of separation between the vaginal wall and the anus.

The pelvic diaphragm has two mechanically different components — a horizontal shelf and a U-shaped sling — and it is the sling that keeps the vagina and rectum closed.

Classification explorer

Components of the pelvic diaphragm

Select a muscle for its origin, insertion and mechanical role.

The levator plate

  • The region of the levator ani between anus and coccyx, formed by the anococcygeal body and iliococcygeal raphe, is clinically called the levator plate.
  • It forms a supportive shelf on which the rectum, upper vagina and uterus rest.
  • Its relatively horizontal position is set by anterior traction from pubococcygeus and puborectalis, and is important to vaginal and uterine support.
Principle

Normal tone in the pelvic diaphragm holds the base of the U close to the backs of the pubic bones, keeping the vagina and rectum closed. Support failure is as much a loss of that resting tone as it is a failure of any ligament.

Innervation

The levator ani is supplied by an anterior branch of the anterior ramus of the third, fourth and fifth sacral nerves — the nerve to the levator ani — which perforates the muscle from its pelvic surface.

Two sphincters, one striated and one smooth, separated by a palpable groove that is the landmark for repair.

External anal sphincter

A single mass of muscle traditionally divided into three parts.

Subcutaneous part

Attached to perianal skin

Forms an encircling ring around the anal canal and is responsible for the radially oriented folds of perianal skin.

Superficial part

Coccyx to perineal body

Attaches to the coccyx posteriorly, contributing to the anococcygeal body, and sends a few fibres into the perineal body anteriorly.

Deep part

Blends with puborectalis

Its fibres generally encircle the rectum and merge indistinguishably with puborectalis, which loops under the dorsal surface of the anorectum.

At third-degree repair

The superficial part forms the bulk of the anal sphincter as it is seen separated in third-degree midline obstetric tears.

Internal anal sphincter

  • A thickening of the circular smooth muscle of the anal wall, lying just inside the external sphincter.
  • Separated from it by a visible intersphincteric groove.
  • Extends downward inside the external sphincter to within a few millimetres of its caudal extent.
  • The longitudinal smooth muscle of the bowel, with some levator ani fibres, descends between the two sphincters in that groove.
A persistent misnomer

At repair of a chronic fourth-degree laceration the internal sphincter can be identified just outside the anal submucosa as a rubbery white layer — which has often been wrongly called fascia during obstetric repair.

Innervation of the sphincters

The external anal sphincter is supplied by the inferior anal (rectal) nerve, which may be a direct branch of the pudendal or arise independently from the sacral plexus; the same nerve gives cutaneous supply to perianal skin and the anal canal down to the pectinate line. The internal anal sphincter is supplied by the inferior hypogastric plexus.

Almost every clinical consequence in this module traces back to one of three things: a torn membrane, a damaged levator, or a divided sphincter.

Structure, failure and clinical expression
StructureHow it failsWhat is seen
Perineal membraneTorn during parturitionAbnormal descent on downward traction of the perineal body; the floor sags and the introitus gapes
Levator aniDamage, with failure of vaginal attachmentsVarying degrees of pelvic organ prolapse
External anal sphincterThird-degree midline obstetric tearSuperficial part separated and visible as the bulk of the sphincter
Internal anal sphincterChronic fourth-degree lacerationRubbery white layer outside the anal submucosa, often mistaken for fascia
Inferior anal (rectal) nerveInjury in the ischioanal fossaFaecal incontinence and pain syndromes
Nerve to levator ani (S3–S5)Perforates the muscle from its pelvic surfaceLoss of the resting tone that holds the hiatus closed
Pearl

Support of the pelvic organs depends on the perineal membrane and the perineal body as much as on the levators — which is why both are discussed with the floor rather than with the viscera.

Do not confuse
  • Pelvic diaphragm = levator ani + ischiococcygeus + their fasciae.
  • Perineal membrane = the triangular sheet below it, formerly called the urogenital diaphragm.
  • Levator hiatus = the whole opening within the U; urogenital hiatus = the part anterior to the perineal body.
Why the fibrous system exists at all

A series of visceral ligaments and fasciae tethers the organs and maintains their position over the closed portions of the levators and their covering fasciae. The openings in the pelvic diaphragm and perineal membrane, required for parturition and elimination, necessitated ancillary fibrous elements concentrated over those open areas to support the viscera where the muscular floor cannot. That fibrous system is covered in Module 5.

Each pelvic organ takes its shape from its neighbours and from its lateral attachments to the pelvic wall — which is why the vaginal lumen is a transverse slit and the bladder is a flattened disc when empty.

120°Vaginal angle at the lower third
7–9 cmAnterior vaginal wall length
7–12 cmUterine tube length
25–30 cmUreteric length
Step walkthrough

The vagina and its relations, in thirds

Step 1 of 3 · Orientation

One cavity, interdependent organs

The vagina is a pliable hollow viscus whose shape is determined by the structures around it and by its lateral attachments to the pelvic wall.

  • Because those attachments are to its lateral margins, the lumen is a transverse slit with anterior and posterior walls in contact.
  • The lower vagina is constricted as it passes through the urogenital hiatus; the upper part is much more capacious.
Step 2 of 3 · Axis

A bend, not a straight tube

Anterior traction from the levator ani bends the vagina through about 120° at the junction of the lower third and upper two-thirds.

  • The cervix typically lies within the anterior vaginal wall, making that wall 2–3 cm shorter than the posterior wall.
  • Anterior wall length is about 7–9 cm, with considerable individual variation.
Step 3 of 3 · Relations

Lower, middle and upper thirds

  • Lower third — fused anteriorly with the urethra, posteriorly with the perineal body, laterally to each levator ani by the fibres of Luschka. The part of pubococcygeus attaching to the vagina is the pubovaginalis.
  • Middle third — vesical neck and trigone anteriorly, rectum posteriorly, levators laterally.
  • Upper third — bladder anteriorly, cul-de-sac posteriorly, cardinal ligaments laterally.
Principle

Each viscus can expand largely independently of its neighbours because their attachments to one another are loose. That property is what creates the surgical cleavage planes covered in Module 5.

Vagina, uterus and cervix are best learned as a single continuous tube whose wall changes character along its length.

Classification explorer

The genital tract, organ by organ

Select an organ for its layers, dimensions and the surgical planes within it.

Pearl

Multiple histological studies over the past hundred years have failed to demonstrate a true fascial layer between bladder and vagina or between vagina and rectum. What the surgeon calls vaginal fascia is the muscularis of the vagina.

Cervical os, canal and the transformation zone

The upper border of the cervical canal is the internal os, above which the narrow canal widens into the endometrial cavity; the lower border is the external os. Squamous epithelium of the vaginal part gives way to columnar epithelium of the canal by squamous metaplasia near the external os. The resulting transformation zone sits variably in relation to the external os and shifts with the hormonal changes of a woman's life.

Where the uterus has no serosa

There is little adventitia in the uterus. The anterior cervix is covered by the bladder and so has no serosa; the broad ligament envelops the lateral aspects of cervix and body, so there is none there either. The posterior cervix does have a serosal covering, because the cul-de-sac peritoneum reflects onto the posterior vaginal wall several centimetres below the cervicovaginal junction.

The broad ligament is a double layer of peritoneum dragged out from the pelvic wall as the müllerian ducts and ovaries migrated to the midline — not a supporting structure.

Mesovarium

Mesentery of the ovary

The ovary is placed dorsally in the consistent arrangement of the three mesenteries.

Mesosalpinx

Mesentery of the tube

The tube lies in the middle and is the most cephalic of the three structures.

Mesoteres

Mesentery of the round ligament

The round ligament is placed ventrally, where it exits the pelvis through the inguinal ligament.

Lateral end

Where the ligament finishes

At the lateral end of tube and ovary the broad ligament ends, where the infundibulopelvic ligament blends with the pelvic wall.

Round ligaments

Extensions of the uterine musculature and the homologue of the gubernaculum testis. They arise as broad bands from each lateral aspect of the anterior corpus, become cylindrical, pass lateral to the deep inferior epigastric vessels into the deep inguinal ring, traverse the canal and enter the subcutaneous tissue of the labium majus. They have little to do with uterine support.

Terminology

Structures at the margins of the broad ligament — including the cardinal and uterosacral ligaments at its lower margin — are visceral ligaments: varying amounts of smooth muscle, vessels, connective tissue and nerves. They are not the pure ligaments of skeletal joints.

The bladder is not layered like a tube but woven, and the functional divide between its dome and its base is a divide in innervation as much as in structure.

Bladder

Wall

A meshwork of intertwining muscle bundles rather than simple layers. The dome is relatively thin when distended; the base is thicker and varies less.

Base

Consists of the trigone and the detrusor loop — a U-shaped band, open posteriorly, forming the bladder base anterior to the intramural ureter. The trigone is smooth muscle arising from the ureters, which occupy two of its three corners.

Vesical neck

Where the urethral lumen traverses the bladder base; the detrusor loop continues as the muscle of the vesical neck and urethra. It rests on the mid vagina.

Shape with filling

Empty, a somewhat flattened disc, slightly concave upward. As it fills, the dome rises off the base and it becomes more spherical.

Principle

Base and dome differ functionally. The base carries α-adrenergic receptors that contract on stimulation and favour continence; the dome responds to β-adrenergic or cholinergic stimulation, contracting to empty the bladder.

Relations

  • Anteriorly — pubic bones and lower abdominal wall.
  • Laterally and inferiorly — pubic bones, abutting obturator internus and levator ani.
  • Posteriorly — vagina and cervix.
  • Apex — joined to the umbilicus by the median umbilical ligament, the urachal remnant.

Urethra

  • Passes through the bladder base for a little under a centimetre as the intramural portion.
  • In its distal two-thirds it is fused with the vagina, sharing derivation from the urogenital sinus.
  • From vesical neck to perineal membrane — which starts at the junction of the middle and distal thirds — the wall has an outer circular skeletal layer (urogenital sphincter) mingling with circular smooth muscle, an inner longitudinal smooth muscle layer, a highly vascular submucosa and oestrogen-responsive nonkeratinised squamous epithelium. The proximal lumen is lined by urothelium.
  • Distal to the perineal membrane the wall is fibrous, forming a nozzle that aims the urinary stream.
Paraurethral glands

Tubular glands in the vascular lamina propria lie on the vaginal surface of the urethra and empty posterolaterally, most prominently over the distal two-thirds. Skene glands are the largest and most distal, draining outside the lumen. Chronic infection can produce urethral diverticula; terminal duct obstruction produces gland cysts, typically lined with stratified squamous epithelium and causing deviation of the urethral opening to the contralateral side.

Ureter — the part within this chapter

A tubular viscus about 25–30 cm long, divided into abdominal and pelvic portions of equal length. The small lumen is surrounded by an inner longitudinal and an outer circular muscle layer. In the abdomen it lies in extraperitoneal connective tissue on the posterior abdominal wall, crossed anteriorly by the left and right colic vessels and the ovarian vessels.

The chapter refers its full course and blood supply to the retroperitoneum section, which was not recoverable from the text extraction used to build these pages — see the build note in the footer.

Innervation of bladder and urethra
  • Bladder — the vesical plexus, a component of the inferior hypogastric plexus.
  • Urethral striated muscle — somatic, via the pudendal nerve or direct branches of the sacral plexus.
  • Urethral smooth muscle — the inferior hypogastric plexus.

The colon changes character three times on its way through the pelvis, and each change has a landmark.

Sigmoid colon

Begins its S-shaped curve at the pelvic brim, with three taeniae coli over a circular smooth muscle layer. Unlike much of the colon it has a definite mesentery in its midportion, of variable length and curvature. Supplied by the sigmoid branches of the inferior mesenteric artery.

Rectum

The colon straightens and becomes rectum, extending from the pelvic brim until it loses its anterior peritoneal investment below the cul-de-sac. Two bands of smooth muscle, anterior and posterior; no taeniae coli.

Transverse rectal folds

Three folds containing mucosa, submucosa and circular muscle. The most prominent is the middle one, lying anteriorly on the right about 8 cm above the anus, which must be negotiated at high rectal examination or sigmoidoscopy.

Rectal ampulla

The rectum expands here as it passes posterior to the vagina, beginning under the cul-de-sac peritoneum and filling the posterior pelvis from the side.

Anorectal junction

Bent at about 90°, pulled ventrally by puborectalis fibres attaching to the pubis and posteriorly by the external anal sphincter's dorsal attachment to the coccyx.

Anus

Thickened circular involuntary muscle as the internal anal sphincter; a series of anal valves; at their lower border the pectinate (dentate) line, where colonic mucosa gives way to non-hair-bearing squamous epithelium before becoming hair-bearing perineal skin at the anocutaneous line.

Relations

Rectum and anus lie against the sacrum and levator plate posteriorly and the vagina anteriorly. Each half of the levator ani abuts the lateral wall and sends fibres to mingle with the longitudinal involuntary fibres between internal and external sphincters.

Arterial supply of the anorectum
ArteryFromTerritory
Superior rectalInferior mesenteric, within the sigmoid mesocolonDivides into two branches at the start of the rectum, ending in the bowel wall
Middle rectalDirect branch of the internal iliac, from the pelvic wall on either sideRectum and ampulla above the pelvic floor
Inferior rectalInternal pudendal, reaching the gut through the ischioanal fossaAnus and external sphincter

A continuous arterial arcade runs along the lateral border of adnexa, uterus and vagina, linking aortic and internal iliac supply end to end.

Arteries

Ovarian

From the aorta, below the renal arteries

Long retroperitoneal course to the cephalic end of the ovary. Running along the ovarian hilum, it also sends vessels through the mesosalpinx to the tube, including a prominent fimbrial branch.

Ovarian veins

Asymmetric drainage

The accompanying venous plexus drains into the vena cava on the right and into the renal vein on the left.

Uterine

From the internal iliac

Sometimes shares an origin with the internal pudendal or vaginal artery. Joins the uterus near the body–cervix junction, though this position varies with traction. Several large uterine veins accompany it.

Vaginal

Two sources, one arcade

The descending (azygous) branch of the uterine artery along the lateral sulci, plus a vaginal branch of the internal iliac, forming an arcade at the 3 and 9 o’clock positions.

Principle

The uterine artery reaches the lateral border of the uterus after passing over the ureter, giving a small branch to it on the way. Its descending branch then crosses the cervicovaginal junction to lie on the side of the vagina.

Additional vaginal supply

  • Branches merge along the anterior and posterior vaginal walls.
  • The distal vagina also receives internal pudendal supply.
  • The posterior wall receives a contribution from the middle and inferior rectal arteries.

Lymphatic drainage

Where each part of the genital tract drains
RegionPrimary nodes
Upper two-thirds of vagina, and uterusObturator, internal iliac and external iliac nodes
Distal-most vaginaWith the vulvar lymphatics, to the inguinal nodes
Uterine corpus — accessory routeAlong the round ligament to the superficial inguinal nodes
Uterus — posterior routeAlong the uterosacral ligaments to the lateral sacral nodes
OvaryFollows the ovarian vessels to the lumbar (para-aortic) chain near the lower abdominal aorta
Innervation

The uterus is supplied by the uterovaginal plexus (Frankenhäuser ganglion), which lies in the connective tissue of the cardinal ligament — the anatomical reason pelvic autonomic injury and parametrial dissection are linked.

Bladder arterial supply

From the superior vesical artery, arising from the patent part of the umbilical artery, and the inferior vesical artery, which is either an independent branch of the internal pudendal artery or arises from the vaginal artery. The urethra receives supply both from an inferior extension of the vesical vessels and from the pudendal vessels.

The tissue connecting the pelvic organs to the pelvic wall behaves like a mesentery: it carries vessels and nerves, and it happens also to support. The spaces between those attachments are what you actually dissect.

3.4 cmMedian dissection at anterior colpotomy
4 cmPosterior cul-de-sac peritoneum on the vaginal wall
2–3 cmRectovaginal space begins above the hymenal ring
4–5 cmRectovaginal space developed below the peritoneal reflection
What it is

Vessels, nerves, meshwork

Blood vessels and nerves interspersed with a supportive meshwork of irregular connective tissue containing collagen and elastin, connecting visceral muscularis to pelvic wall muscles.

What it is not

Not the abdominal ‘fascia’

It is not a layer like the rectus sheath encountered at laparotomy, and the term endopelvic fascia itself remains controversial.

Where it is thickest

Regional smooth muscle

In some areas there is considerable smooth muscle within it — most obviously in the region of the uterosacral ligaments.

Honest caveat

Separable, not separate

These layers can be separated from the viscera, much as superficial bowel wall can be artificially separated from deeper layers — but they are not themselves separate structures.

Principle

The word ligament is doing three different jobs in the pelvis: a dense band linking two bones, a ridge in the peritoneum, and a thickening of the endopelvic fascia. The genital tract ligaments are mostly the last two.

Scope of these pages

The source chapter continues past the rectovaginal space into the sacrospinous ligament region, the retroperitoneal spaces and lateral pelvic wall, structures above the pelvic brim, the presacral space and the pelvic lymphatics. That material was not recoverable from the text used to build these modules and is therefore not represented here.

Condensations of visceral fascia on the lateral walls of the organs transmit their neurovascular supply and, in doing so, separate one surgical cleavage plane from the next.

Step walkthrough

From cleavage plane to cul-de-sac

Step 1 of 3 · The planes

Spaces are filled, not empty

Pelvic organs expand largely independently of one another because their attachments are loose, so they separate easily along lines of cleavage.

  • These cleavage planes are called spaces, but they contain fatty or areolar connective tissue.
  • They are separated from one another by the connections of the viscera to each other and to the pelvic walls.
Step 2 of 3 · Cul-de-sacs

Front and back behave differently

Properly the vesicouterine and rectouterine pouches.

  • Anteriorly the peritoneum lies several centimetres above the vagina; it is loosely applied, forming the vesicouterine fold that lifts to create a bladder flap.
  • Posteriorly the peritoneum covers the vagina, extending about 4 cm along the posterior wall below the fornix.
  • That posterior arrangement allows direct peritoneal entry from the vagina at vaginal hysterectomy, culdocentesis or colpotomy.
Step 3 of 3 · Suspension

The mesenteries of the genital tract

At the base of the broad ligament, beginning just caudal to the uterine arteries, a thickening of endopelvic fascia attaches cervix and upper vagina to the pelvic side walls.

  • Comprising the cardinal and uterosacral ligaments — the parametrium and paracervix.
  • They are mesenteries transmitting vessels and nerves from the pelvic walls to the genital tract, not bone-to-bone bands.
Pearl

The endopelvic fascia has a supportive function as well as a conduit function — it is analogous to a mesentery connecting bowel to body wall. Understanding its disposition matters equally in vaginal and abdominal surgery.

One continuous sheet of tissue carries four different names depending on which part you are looking at and what it attaches to.

Parametrium, paracervix and paracolpium — who attaches to what
TermRefers to
Uterosacral ligamentThe portion forming the medial and posterior margin of the parametrium, bordering the rectouterine pouch (cul-de-sac of Douglas)
Cardinal ligamentThe portion attaching the lateral margins of cervix and vagina to the pelvic walls
ParametriumAll the tissue attaching to the uterus — both cardinal and uterosacral ligaments
ParacolpiumThe portion attaching to the vagina — the cardinal ligament of the vagina
Broad ligamentPeritoneal folds extending laterally from the uterus over the adnexa. No supportive function
Principle

The course of the ureter, as it forms a tunnel between the cardinal and uterosacral ligaments, is the point of division between those two structures.

Composition differs between the two

Uterosacral

Predominantly smooth muscle

With the autonomic nerves of the pelvic organs and some intermixed connective tissue and blood vessels.

Cardinal

Predominantly perivascular

Perivascular connective tissue, nerves and pelvic vessels surrounding the uterine and vaginal arteries and veins.

Uterosacral attachment

Discrete, then fanned

Discrete near the cervix, fanning out in the retroperitoneal layer to a broad, ill-defined attachment over the second, third and fourth sacral segments.

Cardinal attachment

Onto piriformis

Attaches to the cervix below the isthmus and fans out onto the pelvic walls over the piriformis muscle in the region of the greater sciatic foramen.

Orientation pearl

The cardinal ligaments are often drawn extending laterally from the cervix, but in the standing position they are almost vertical — as you would expect of suspensory tissue.

Surgical boundary

At radical pelvic surgery, the cardinal ligaments form the boundary between the anterior paravesical space and the posterior pararectal space. The uterosacral ligaments hold the cervix posteriorly over the levator plate.

Failure of the vagina’s attachments, together with levator ani damage, produces prolapse — and which segment fails determines which repair is appropriate.

Anterior compartment

  • Comprises the anterior vaginal wall and its endopelvic fascia attachments to the pelvic sidewall at the tendinous arch of the pelvic fascia.
  • Between vagina and bladder lies the vesicovaginal space; between cervix and bladder the vesicocervical space.
  • These two are separated only by the attachment of the anterior vaginal wall to the cervix and by augmented bands attaching the lower pole of the bladder to the anterior cervix — often called the supravaginal septum.
Principle

At anterior colpotomy for vaginal hysterectomy, the median dissection distance from the initial incision at the cervicovaginal junction to the anterior peritoneal reflection is about 3.4 cm.

Posterior compartment

Upper third

Supported by the uterosacral ligaments and bounded posteriorly by the cul-de-sac.

Middle

The rectovaginal space begins distal to the cul-de-sac peritoneum and extends down to the perineal body. Histologically a loose fibroadipose layer with slightly interspersed bands of fibrous tissue.

Distal third

Separated from the anal wall by the perineal body, which includes the anal sphincter muscles. No histological plane of separation exists here between vaginal wall and anus.

Failure patterns

Rectocele, enterocele, perineal bulge, or a combination — partly explained by defect location and by changes in the associated muscle, connective tissue and nerves.

Repairs

Identifying loss of support at distal, mid or proximal segments directs the choice between perineorrhaphy, posterior colporrhaphy and sacral colpoperineopexy.

The rectovaginal fascia question

Descriptions of the tissue between vagina and rectum vary, but there is growing consensus that there is no true rectovaginal fascia or Denonvilliers fascia. Despite the histological findings, the Terminologia Anatomica still includes the term.

What is actually plicated at posterior colporrhaphy

The rectovaginal space can generally be developed without difficulty below the posterior peritoneal reflection for 4–5 cm to the level of the perineal body apex. No discrete separate fascial layer has been demonstrated, but lateral projections of vaginal adventitia to the endopelvic fascia, pelvic sidewall connective tissue and levator ani muscles have been consistently observed.

The tissue plicated at posterior colporrhaphy is therefore likely derived from a splitting of the posterior vaginal wall — muscularis and adventitia — and/or the anterior rectal wall. Gross examination misleads: handling the tissue can artificially create a layer that is then misconstrued as a separate fascia.

Five named planes account for most pelvic dissection, and each is defined by the attachments that bound it rather than by anything it contains.

Classification explorer

The extraperitoneal surgical spaces

Select a space for its boundaries, contents and the operations that use it.

Pearl

Keeping the anterior–posterior asymmetry in mind — peritoneum well above the vagina in front, directly on the vagina behind — is what facilitates entering both cul-de-sacs at vaginal hysterectomy.

Bleeding in the retropubic space

The vesical venous plexus lies lateral to the bladder and vesical neck, and the dorsal veins of the clitoris drain into it. These veins bleed when sutures are placed in paravaginal and paravesical tissue, but the ooze usually stops when the sutures are tied. Dissection over the superior pubic rami should be careful, because accessory obturator connections are commonly present there.

Urethral support is real but secondary: the primary determinant of stress incontinence is the strength of the sphincter mechanism.

Principle

It was previously thought that urethral support was the primary factor determining stress incontinence. More recent work shows the strength of the urethral sphincter mechanism — low urethral closure pressure — is primary, with support playing a secondary role.

How the support layer works

Distal urethra

Inseparable from the vagina because of their shared derivation from the urogenital sinus. Fixed in position by connections of the periurethral tissues and vagina to the pubic bones through the perineal membrane.

From the midurethra upward

A hammock-like layer of endopelvic fascia and anterior vaginal wall supports the proximal urethra.

Lateral stabilisation

By attachments to both the tendinous arch of the pelvic fascia and the medial margin of the levator ani muscles.

Dynamic element

Because the endopelvic fascia attaches to muscle, levator contraction and relaxation elevate the urethra and let it descend.

On straining

Raised abdominal pressure on the ventral surface of the urethra compresses it closed against that layer. An unyielding layer is a firm backstop; an unstable one compromises closure.

Why the attachments matter more than the tissue

The stability of the supportive layer — not its bulk — determines the effectiveness of closure. The integrity of the attachment to the tendinous arch of the fascia and the levator ani is therefore critical to the stress continence mechanism.

Where this connects to the rest of the chapter

The same tendinous arch appears in the anterior vaginal compartment as the sidewall attachment of the anterior vaginal wall, and in the retropubic space as the dorsolateral limit of that space. The levator ani whose medial margin stabilises the hammock is the pubovisceral muscle described in Module 3, and the perineal membrane fixing the distal urethra is the sheet covered there as well.

Source: Corton MM, DeLancey JOL. Surgical Anatomy of the Female Pelvis. In: Te Linde’s Operative Gynecology, Chapter 1.
